    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/codebase/upstream-issues",
    "content": "# LiteLLM #24720: latency routing loses concurrent measurements\n\n- Status at capture: open\n- Upstream: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24720\n- Pinned source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`\n\nUnder concurrent completions, latency-based routing can collapse into a random\nselection weighted by deployment count. `async_log_success_event` in\n`litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` reads an entire cached deployment\nmap, mutates one entry, and writes the whole map back. Concurrent callbacks can\nread the same snapshot and overwrite one another, dropping measurements for\nother deployments.\n\nAcceptance criteria:\n\n1. A deterministic concurrency test demonstrates the lost update.\n2. Concurrent success callbacks preserve measurements for every deployment.\n3. The fix does not hold a process-wide lock across network I/O.\n4. Existing selection and expiration behavior remains intact.\n\n",

# LiteLLM #24720: latency routing loses concurrent measurements

- Status at capture: open
- Upstream: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24720
- Pinned source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

Under concurrent completions, latency-based routing can collapse into a random
selection weighted by deployment count. `async_log_success_event` in
`litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` reads an entire cached deployment
map, mutates one entry, and writes the whole map back. Concurrent callbacks can
read the same snapshot and overwrite one another, dropping measurements for
other deployments.

Acceptance criteria:

1. A deterministic concurrency test demonstrates the lost update.
2. Concurrent success callbacks preserve measurements for every deployment.
3. The fix does not hold a process-wide lock across network I/O.
4. Existing selection and expiration behavior remains intact.

@pytest.mark.parametrize("sync_mode", [True, False])

async def test_latency_memory_leak(sync_mode):
    """
    Test to make sure there's no memory leak caused by lowest latency routing

    - make 10 calls -> check memory
    - make 11th call -> no change in memory
    """
    test_cache = DualCache()
    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(router_cache=test_cache)
    model_group = "gpt-3.5-turbo"
    deployment_id = "1234"
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": "gpt-3.5-turbo",
                "deployment": "azure/gpt-4.1-mini",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }
    start_time = time.time()
    response_obj = {"usage": {"total_tokens": 50}}
    time.sleep(5)
    end_time = time.time()
    for _ in range(10):
        if sync_mode:
            lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
                response_obj=response_obj,
                kwargs=kwargs,
                start_time=start_time,
                end_time=end_time,
            )
        else:
            await lowest_latency_logger.async_log_success_event(
                response_obj=response_obj,
                kwargs=kwargs,
                start_time=start_time,
                end_time=end_time,
            )
    latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"
    cache_value = copy.deepcopy(
        test_cache.get_cache(key=latency_key)
    )  # MAKE SURE NO MEMORY LEAK IN CACHING OBJECT

    if sync_mode:
        lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,
            end_time=end_time,
        )
    else:
        await lowest_latency_logger.async_log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,
            end_time=end_time,
        )
    new_cache_value = test_cache.get_cache(key=latency_key)
    # Assert that the size of the cache doesn't grow unreasonably
    assert get_size(new_cache_value) <= get_size(
        cache_value
    ), f"Memory leak detected in function call! new_cache size={get_size(new_cache_value)}, old cache size={get_size(cache_value)}"


def get_size(obj, seen=None):
    # From https://goshippo.com/blog/measure-real-size-any-python-object/
    # Recursively finds size of objects
    size = sys.getsizeof(obj)
    if seen is None:
        seen = set()
    obj_id = id(obj)
    if obj_id in seen:
        return 0
    seen.add(obj_id)
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        size += sum([get_size(v, seen) for v in obj.values()])
        size += sum([get_size(k, seen) for k in obj.keys()])
    elif hasattr(obj, "__dict__"):
        size += get_size(obj.__dict__, seen)
    elif hasattr(obj, "__iter__") and not isinstance(obj, (str, bytes, bytearray)):
        size += sum([get_size(i, seen) for i in obj])
    return size

async def _deploy(lowest_latency_logger, deployment_id, tokens_used, duration):
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": "gpt-3.5-turbo",
                "deployment": "azure/gpt-4.1-mini",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }
    start_time = time.time()
    response_obj = {"usage": {"total_tokens": tokens_used}}
    await asyncio.sleep(duration)
    end_time = time.time()
    lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
        response_obj=response_obj,
        kwargs=kwargs,
        start_time=start_time,
        end_time=end_time,
    )


async def _gather_deploy(all_deploys):
    return await asyncio.gather(*[_deploy(*t) for t in all_deploys])

def test_latency_list_trimming_discards_oldest_entry():
    """
    When the latency list reaches max_latency_list_size, the oldest entry is
    discarded to make room for new entries. The newest entry is appended at
    the end of the list.
    """
    max_size = 3
    test_cache = DualCache()
    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(
        router_cache=test_cache, routing_args={"max_latency_list_size": max_size}
    )

    model_group = "gpt-3.5-turbo"
    deployment_id = "test-deployment"
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": model_group,
                "deployment": "azure/gpt-4.1-mini",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }

    # With 1 completion token, the logged latency value equals the raw
    # response time, so we can use distinct, identifiable values.
    latencies_to_add = []
    for i in range(max_size + 1):  # One more than max to trigger trimming
        start_time = time.time()
        response_obj = {"usage": {"total_tokens": 1, "completion_tokens": 1}}
        expected_latency = float(i + 1)  # 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0
        end_time = start_time + expected_latency
        latencies_to_add.append(expected_latency)

        lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,
            end_time=end_time,
        )

    latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"
    cached_data = test_cache.get_cache(key=latency_key)
    latency_list = cached_data[deployment_id]["latency"]

    assert (
        len(latency_list) == max_size
    ), f"Expected {max_size} entries, got {len(latency_list)}"

    newest_latency = latencies_to_add[-1]  # 4.0
    oldest_latency = latencies_to_add[0]  # 1.0
    tolerance = 0.1

    # Newest entry is at the end of the list.
    assert (
        abs(latency_list[-1] - newest_latency) < tolerance
    ), f"Newest latency {newest_latency} should be at end, got {latency_list[-1]}"

    # Oldest entry is no longer in the list.
    for latency in latency_list:
        assert (
            abs(latency - oldest_latency) > tolerance
        ), f"Oldest latency {oldest_latency} should have been discarded, found {latency}"

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_timeout_penalty_discards_oldest_entry():
    """
    Timeout penalties (1000.0) are appended to the latency list and, when the
    list is full, the oldest entry is discarded.
    """
    max_size = 3
    test_cache = DualCache()
    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(
        router_cache=test_cache, routing_args={"max_latency_list_size": max_size}
    )

    model_group = "gpt-3.5-turbo"
    deployment_id = "test-deployment"
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": model_group,
                "deployment": "azure/gpt-4.1-mini",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }

    # Fill the list with max_size normal latency entries first.
    for i in range(max_size):
        start_time = time.time()
        response_obj = {"usage": {"total_tokens": 1, "completion_tokens": 1}}
        end_time = start_time + float(i + 1)

        await lowest_latency_logger.async_log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,
            end_time=end_time,
        )

    # Trigger a timeout failure: this appends 1000.0 and should discard the
    # oldest normal entry (1.0).
    timeout_kwargs = {
        **kwargs,
        "exception": litellm.Timeout(
            message="Request timed out", model="test-model", llm_provider="test"
        ),
    }

    await lowest_latency_logger.async_log_failure_event(
        kwargs=timeout_kwargs,
        response_obj=None,
        start_time=time.time(),
        end_time=time.time() + 30,
    )

    latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"
    cached_data = await test_cache.async_get_cache(key=latency_key)
    latency_list = cached_data[deployment_id]["latency"]

    assert len(latency_list) == max_size

    # Timeout penalty is the newest entry.
    assert (
        latency_list[-1] == 1000.0
    ), f"Timeout penalty should be at end of list, got {latency_list[-1]}"

    # Oldest normal entry (1.0) has been discarded.
    tolerance = 0.1
    for latency in latency_list[:-1]:
        assert (
            abs(latency - 1.0) > tolerance
        ), f"Oldest latency 1.0 should have been discarded, found {latency}"

    """

    in insertion order (oldest at index 0, newest at index -1).
    """
    max_size = 3
    test_cache = DualCache()
    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(
        router_cache=test_cache, routing_args={"max_latency_list_size": max_size}

            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }

    # Add 10 entries (7 more than max) to trigger multiple trims.
    all_latencies = []

    assert len(latency_list) == max_size

    # After inserting 1..10 with max_size=3, the list should be [8, 9, 10].

    for i, expected in enumerate(expected_remaining):
        assert (
            abs(latency_list[i] - expected) < tolerance
        ), f"At index {i}, expected ~{expected}, got {latency_list[i]}"

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Per-model latency SLOs and alerting policy (perf canary)\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-sre\",\n  \"author\": \"Aisha Bello\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-15\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-20\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Sean Gallagher\",\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Allison Grant\",\n    \"Noah Patel\",\n    \"Sofia Ivanova\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"sre\",\n    \"slo\",\n    \"latency\",\n    \"performance\",\n    \"perf-canary\",\n    \"alerting\",\n    \"oncall\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/perf-regression-canary-design.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-perf-canary-baseline-and-thresholds.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/perf-canary-dashboards-spec.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/perf-canary-overhead-and-safety-standards.json\"\n  ],\n  \"body\": \"## Purpose\\nThis page defines Redwood\\u2019s alerting policy for **per-model performance regressions** detected by the production **perf-canary**. It maps canary signals to SRE-style concepts (SLOs, error budgets, paging hygiene), establishes **warning vs paging** thresholds, and documents **notification routing and ownership**.\\n\\nThis is intentionally *not* a customer-facing SLA document. It is an internal policy for protecting production serving performance and keeping on-call load manageable.\\n\\n## Scope\\nIn scope:\\n- Perf-canary synthetic workload measurements per model (and optionally per region/tier/SKU as configured).\\n- Alerting for **p95 latency regressions** and **tokens/sec drops**, plus attribution breakouts (queueing vs runtime execution).\\n- Routing rules for #eng-runtime, #eng-oncall, and incident-bot.\\n\\nOut of scope:\\n- Customer prompt shadowing or any alerting tied to customer content.\\n- Quality regression signals (owned by Applied ML / eval harness).\\n\\n## Key concepts and definitions\\n### What we mean by \\u201cSLO\\u201d here\\nPerformance regressions are treated as an **SLO-like reliability signal**:\\n- The intent is to detect and respond quickly to regressions that would materially impact customers.\\n- Because perf-canary traffic is synthetic and small, it does not measure customer experience directly. It is a **leading indicator**.\\n\\nWe therefore use a two-tier policy:\\n- **Warning alerts**: actionable but non-paging; used to catch early drift and support rapid triage.\\n- **Paging alerts**: reserved for sustained, high-confidence regressions on **top models** or broad infra/runtime events.\\n\\n### Primary signals\\nAll alerts are computed as deviations from a stored baseline for the tuple:\\n- model + model_version\\n- runtime_build_id\\n- hardware_sku\\n- region (optional; enabled when variance differs by region)\\n\\nPrimary regressions:\\n- **Latency**: p95 end-to-end latency (ms) and, where available, runtime-only p95 (ms)\\n- **Throughput**: tokens/sec (aggregate and per-request where applicable)\\n\\nAttribution / triage signals (non-primary, used in dashboards and incident context):\\n- queueing time p95\\n- prefill latency p95\\n- decode latency p95\\n- batch size distribution\\n- KV cache hit rate (where applicable)\\n\\n## Ownership and responsibilities\\n### Owning teams\\n- **Primary owner (engineering)**: Serving Runtime\\n  - Responsible for kernel/scheduler regressions, runtime build issues, and canary-service correctness.\\n  - Tech lead: Noah Patel\\n  - Kernel escalation: Hiro Tanaka\\n  - Scheduling escalation: Sofia Ivanova\\n- **SRE owner (engineering)**: SRE\\n  - Responsible for alerting policy, paging hygiene, on-call readiness, incident workflow, and coordination.\\n  - SRE sponsor: Sean Gallagher\\n  - Routing/incident hygiene: Rafael Mendes\\n- **Platform Telemetry (engineering)**\\n  - Responsible for metrics pipeline latency/availability and label cardinality guardrails.\\n  - Lead: Logan Wright\\n\\n### Expectations\\n- Warnings should be acknowledged (Slack reaction or short reply) by runtime within business hours.\\n- Paging incidents must be actively managed by the on-call (SRE primary) with runtime engaged as needed.\\n- Any change that affects baselines (kernel selection changes, scheduler batching heuristics, fleet SKU swaps, region migrations) must be announced per change-management guidance below.\\n\\n## Alert tiers and policy\\n### Tier 0: Informational (no alerts)\\nUsed for new models/regions during ramp-up:\\n- Dashboards visible, no Slack alerts.\\n- Goal: characterize variance and choose thresholds.\\n\\n### Tier 1: Warning (non-paging)\\n**Intent:** catch regressions early with low disruption.\\n\\nRouting:\\n- Delivered by incident-bot to **#eng-runtime** (threaded, deduped).\\n- Mention: @runtime-perf-canary (group) only; no paging.\\n\\nPolicy:\\n- Requires minimum sample size and sustained window (see anti-flap).\\n- Includes dashboard links + baseline/observed values + likely attribution hint (queueing vs runtime-only).\\n\\nDefault warning triggers (per model tuple; may be overridden per model):\\n- p95 end-to-end latency: **>= +10%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**\\n- tokens/sec: **<= -8%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**\\n- runtime-only p95 latency (if available): **>= +10%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**\\n\\nNotes:\\n- Warning thresholds are intentionally sensitive to support release validation.\\n- If warnings are noisy for a model, tune via per-model thresholds rather than disabling globally.\\n\\n### Tier 2: Paging (Sev2)\\n**Intent:** high-confidence regression likely to impact customers or block a rollout.\\n\\nRouting:\\n- Page **#eng-oncall** via incident-bot (Sev2).\\n- Auto-create incident thread in **#incidents** with runbook link.\\n- Runtime is auto-mentioned in incident thread (not paged by default unless escalation criteria met).\\n\\nEligibility (any one):\\n- Model is classified as a **Top Model** (see \\u201cModel criticality\\u201d below)\\n- Regression is detected across **multiple models** consistent with infra/runtime-wide issue\\n- Regression coincides with an active rollout gate (release in progress)\\n\\nDefault paging triggers:\\n- Top model p95 latency: **>= +20%** vs baseline for **30 minutes**\\n- Top model tokens/sec: **<= -15%** vs baseline for **30 minutes**\\n- Multi-model event: **>= 3 models** in warning state with a shared dimension (same region+SKU or same runtime_build_id) for **20 minutes**\\n\\n### Tier 3: Paging (Sev1) \\u2014 rare\\n**Intent:** severe widespread regression or inability to serve within expected performance envelope.\\n\\nRouting:\\n- Page #eng-oncall (Sev1) and engage runtime on-call immediately.\\n\\nDefault Sev1 triggers:\\n- Top model p95 latency: **>= +35%** vs baseline for **20 minutes** AND trend is worsening\\n- tokens/sec drop: **<= -25%** vs baseline for **20 minutes** on top model(s)\\n- Broad outage-like performance event across regions or across a majority of top models\\n\\n## Model criticality classification\\nPerf-canary configuration assigns each model to a criticality bucket:\\n- **Top model**: high traffic and/or enterprise-critical; paging enabled once tuned.\\n- **High-risk model**: newly onboarded, recent kernel/scheduler change, or recent fleet move; warnings enabled early, paging after variance understood.\\n- **Standard**: covered by canary; warnings only unless part of a multi-model event.\\n\\nThe current list lives in control-plane config and is audited (see perf-canary design doc).\\n\\n## Anti-flap, confidence, and minimum data requirements\\nTo reduce false positives and alert storms, all alert tiers must meet these conditions:\\n\\n### Minimum sample size\\n- Default: **>= 200 canary requests** per model tuple in the evaluation window\\n- AND at least **3 prompt-length buckets** represented (to avoid bias)\\n\\nIf a model\\u2019s canary QPS is intentionally lower, use model-specific thresholds (do not lower min-samples globally).\\n\\n### Sustained windows\\n- Warning: sustained for **15 minutes** (rolling)\\n- Paging: sustained for **30 minutes** (rolling)\\n\\n### Dedupe keys\\nIncident-bot dedupes by:\\n- model + model_version\\n- region\\n- hardware_sku\\n- runtime_build_id\\n- regression_type (latency vs throughput)\\n\\n### Alert reset / recovery\\nAn alert is considered recovered when the signal returns within:\\n- latency: **<= +5%** of baseline for **20 minutes**\\n- tokens/sec: **>= -5%** of baseline for **20 minutes**\\n\\n## Notification routing matrix\\n| Condition | Alert tier | Primary channel | Who acts | Escalation |\\n|---|---:|---|---|---|\\n| Single model, mild regression | Warning | #eng-runtime | Runtime (business hours) | SRE if sustained > 4h or release ongoing |\\n| Top model sustained regression | Sev2 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call + Runtime | Escalate to kernel/scheduling owners based on attribution |\\n| Multi-model / infra-shaped regression | Sev2 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call (coordination) | Infra/Fleet (Vanessa Ortiz) + Telemetry (Logan Wright) |\\n| Severe widespread regression | Sev1 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call + Runtime on-call | Eng leadership per incident policy |\\n\\n## Triage guidance (what the alerts should tell you)\\nEvery perf-canary alert payload must include:\\n- model + version + runtime_build_id + region + hardware_sku\\n- baseline value + observed value + percent change\\n- sample count and evaluation window\\n- attribution hints (if available): queueing delta, runtime-only delta, batch size shift\\n- links:\\n  - Grafana: per-model dashboard\\n  - Traces/logs: canary request traces (synthetic)\\n  - Runbook: runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert\\n\\nIf the alert does not include these fields, treat as a tooling bug and file against telemetry/canary.\\n\\n## Mapping to rollout gates\\nPerf-canary signals are used as a **gate** for runtime releases and high-risk model rollouts.\\n\\nPolicy:\\n- During a rollout, **Warning alerts on gated models** require explicit acknowledgement by release captain and runtime TL.\\n- **Sev2+ paging alerts** on gated models automatically trigger a \\u201cpause rollout\\u201d action (owned by Release Engineering integration) unless the incident commander overrides with a documented reason.\\n\\nOverride guidance:\\n- Only override if the regression is confirmed to be canary-only (e.g., telemetry lag, known baseline artifact) and mitigation is in progress.\\n\\n## Change management and baseline integrity\\n### Changes that require a baseline note\\nWhen any of the following occurs, the change owner must post a brief note in #eng-runtime (and link in the release ticket):\\n- runtime build changes affecting scheduling, batching, kernels, memory management\\n- kernel selection/auto-tuning updates\\n- fleet changes: new GPU SKU, driver/runtime stack changes, power caps, MIG changes\\n- region capacity tier changes that alter queueing behavior\\n\\n### Baseline updates\\nBaseline update policy is documented in the ADR. Operationally:\\n- Baselines are versioned and tied to runtime_build_id and hardware_sku.\\n- Baseline updates must be intentional; avoid \\u201csilent\\u201d rolling baselines that mask regressions.\\n- If a baseline must be refreshed (e.g., intentional perf improvement), update is done via baseline pipeline and recorded in the change log.\\n\\n## Paging hygiene and review cadence\\n- SRE reviews paging volume weekly during rollout phases; goal is **< 2 perf-canary pages/week** outside planned rollouts.\\n- Any paging false positive requires:\\n  - a short incident note in the incident thread\\n  - a follow-up ticket to fix root cause (thresholds, dedupe, baseline, telemetry)\\n- Thresholds are revisited:\\n  - after each major runtime release\\n  - after introducing a new top model\\n  - after a fleet SKU transition\\n\\n## Appendix A: Default threshold summary\\nThese defaults apply unless overridden per model/region/SKU.\\n\\n- Warning:\\n  - p95 latency +10% for 15m (>=200 samples)\\n  - tokens/sec -8% for 15m (>=200 samples)\\n- Sev2 (Top models):\\n  - p95 latency +20% for 30m\\n  - tokens/sec -15% for 30m\\n- Sev1 (Top models):\\n  - p95 latency +35% for 20m\\n  - tokens/sec -25% for 20m\\n\\n## Appendix B: Where to find things\\n- Dashboards: see \\u201cperf-canary dashboards spec\\u201d (linked above)\\n- Runbook: runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert\\n- Baseline/threshold ADR: adr-perf-canary-baseline-and-thresholds\\n- Overhead/safety: perf-canary-overhead-and-safety-standards\\n\\n## Changelog\\n- 2026-02-20: Tightened dedupe keys and clarified multi-model paging eligibility (post initial rollout tuning).\\n- 2026-02-03: Added minimum bucket diversity requirement; clarified recovery criteria.\\n- 2026-01-15: Initial publication.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_6d5cbbe19ee94f4c882a2213ed3ab2a8\"\n}",

{
  "title": "Per-model latency SLOs and alerting policy (perf canary)",
  "space": "eng-sre",
  "author": "Aisha Bello",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-15",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-20",
  "reviewers": [
    "Sean Gallagher",
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Allison Grant",
    "Noah Patel",
    "Sofia Ivanova"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "sre",
    "slo",
    "latency",
    "performance",
    "perf-canary",
    "alerting",
    "oncall"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/perf-regression-canary-design.json",
    "sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-perf-canary-baseline-and-thresholds.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/perf-canary-dashboards-spec.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert.json",
    "sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/perf-canary-overhead-and-safety-standards.json"
  ],
  "body": "## Purpose
This page defines Redwood’s alerting policy for **per-model performance regressions** detected by the production **perf-canary**. It maps canary signals to SRE-style concepts (SLOs, error budgets, paging hygiene), establishes **warning vs paging** thresholds, and documents **notification routing and ownership**.

This is intentionally *not* a customer-facing SLA document. It is an internal policy for protecting production serving performance and keeping on-call load manageable.

## Scope
In scope:
- Perf-canary synthetic workload measurements per model (and optionally per region/tier/SKU as configured).
- Alerting for **p95 latency regressions** and **tokens/sec drops**, plus attribution breakouts (queueing vs runtime execution).
- Routing rules for #eng-runtime, #eng-oncall, and incident-bot.

Out of scope:
- Customer prompt shadowing or any alerting tied to customer content.
- Quality regression signals (owned by Applied ML / eval harness).

## Key concepts and definitions
### What we mean by “SLO” here
Performance regressions are treated as an **SLO-like reliability signal**:
- The intent is to detect and respond quickly to regressions that would materially impact customers.
- Because perf-canary traffic is synthetic and small, it does not measure customer experience directly. It is a **leading indicator**.

We therefore use a two-tier policy:
- **Warning alerts**: actionable but non-paging; used to catch early drift and support rapid triage.
- **Paging alerts**: reserved for sustained, high-confidence regressions on **top models** or broad infra/runtime events.

### Primary signals
All alerts are computed as deviations from a stored baseline for the tuple:
- model + model_version
- runtime_build_id
- hardware_sku
- region (optional; enabled when variance differs by region)

Primary regressions:
- **Latency**: p95 end-to-end latency (ms) and, where available, runtime-only p95 (ms)
- **Throughput**: tokens/sec (aggregate and per-request where applicable)

Attribution / triage signals (non-primary, used in dashboards and incident context):
- queueing time p95
- prefill latency p95
- decode latency p95
- batch size distribution
- KV cache hit rate (where applicable)

## Ownership and responsibilities
### Owning teams
- **Primary owner (engineering)**: Serving Runtime
  - Responsible for kernel/scheduler regressions, runtime build issues, and canary-service correctness.
  - Tech lead: Noah Patel
  - Kernel escalation: Hiro Tanaka
  - Scheduling escalation: Sofia Ivanova
- **SRE owner (engineering)**: SRE
  - Responsible for alerting policy, paging hygiene, on-call readiness, incident workflow, and coordination.
  - SRE sponsor: Sean Gallagher
  - Routing/incident hygiene: Rafael Mendes
- **Platform Telemetry (engineering)**
  - Responsible for metrics pipeline latency/availability and label cardinality guardrails.
  - Lead: Logan Wright

### Expectations
- Warnings should be acknowledged (Slack reaction or short reply) by runtime within business hours.
- Paging incidents must be actively managed by the on-call (SRE primary) with runtime engaged as needed.
- Any change that affects baselines (kernel selection changes, scheduler batching heuristics, fleet SKU swaps, region migrations) must be announced per change-management guidance below.

## Alert tiers and policy
### Tier 0: Informational (no alerts)
Used for new models/regions during ramp-up:
- Dashboards visible, no Slack alerts.
- Goal: characterize variance and choose thresholds.

### Tier 1: Warning (non-paging)
**Intent:** catch regressions early with low disruption.

Routing:
- Delivered by incident-bot to **#eng-runtime** (threaded, deduped).
- Mention: @runtime-perf-canary (group) only; no paging.

Policy:
- Requires minimum sample size and sustained window (see anti-flap).
- Includes dashboard links + baseline/observed values + likely attribution hint (queueing vs runtime-only).

Default warning triggers (per model tuple; may be overridden per model):
- p95 end-to-end latency: **>= +10%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**
- tokens/sec: **<= -8%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**
- runtime-only p95 latency (if available): **>= +10%** vs baseline for **15 minutes**

Notes:
- Warning thresholds are intentionally sensitive to support release validation.
- If warnings are noisy for a model, tune via per-model thresholds rather than disabling globally.

### Tier 2: Paging (Sev2)
**Intent:** high-confidence regression likely to impact customers or block a rollout.

Routing:
- Page **#eng-oncall** via incident-bot (Sev2).
- Auto-create incident thread in **#incidents** with runbook link.
- Runtime is auto-mentioned in incident thread (not paged by default unless escalation criteria met).

Eligibility (any one):
- Model is classified as a **Top Model** (see “Model criticality” below)
- Regression is detected across **multiple models** consistent with infra/runtime-wide issue
- Regression coincides with an active rollout gate (release in progress)

Default paging triggers:
- Top model p95 latency: **>= +20%** vs baseline for **30 minutes**
- Top model tokens/sec: **<= -15%** vs baseline for **30 minutes**
- Multi-model event: **>= 3 models** in warning state with a shared dimension (same region+SKU or same runtime_build_id) for **20 minutes**

### Tier 3: Paging (Sev1) — rare
**Intent:** severe widespread regression or inability to serve within expected performance envelope.

Routing:
- Page #eng-oncall (Sev1) and engage runtime on-call immediately.

Default Sev1 triggers:
- Top model p95 latency: **>= +35%** vs baseline for **20 minutes** AND trend is worsening
- tokens/sec drop: **<= -25%** vs baseline for **20 minutes** on top model(s)
- Broad outage-like performance event across regions or across a majority of top models

## Model criticality classification
Perf-canary configuration assigns each model to a criticality bucket:
- **Top model**: high traffic and/or enterprise-critical; paging enabled once tuned.
- **High-risk model**: newly onboarded, recent kernel/scheduler change, or recent fleet move; warnings enabled early, paging after variance understood.
- **Standard**: covered by canary; warnings only unless part of a multi-model event.

The current list lives in control-plane config and is audited (see perf-canary design doc).

## Anti-flap, confidence, and minimum data requirements
To reduce false positives and alert storms, all alert tiers must meet these conditions:

### Minimum sample size
- Default: **>= 200 canary requests** per model tuple in the evaluation window
- AND at least **3 prompt-length buckets** represented (to avoid bias)

If a model’s canary QPS is intentionally lower, use model-specific thresholds (do not lower min-samples globally).

### Sustained windows
- Warning: sustained for **15 minutes** (rolling)
- Paging: sustained for **30 minutes** (rolling)

### Dedupe keys
Incident-bot dedupes by:
- model + model_version
- region
- hardware_sku
- runtime_build_id
- regression_type (latency vs throughput)

### Alert reset / recovery
An alert is considered recovered when the signal returns within:
- latency: **<= +5%** of baseline for **20 minutes**
- tokens/sec: **>= -5%** of baseline for **20 minutes**

## Notification routing matrix
| Condition | Alert tier | Primary channel | Who acts | Escalation |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Single model, mild regression | Warning | #eng-runtime | Runtime (business hours) | SRE if sustained > 4h or release ongoing |
| Top model sustained regression | Sev2 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call + Runtime | Escalate to kernel/scheduling owners based on attribution |
| Multi-model / infra-shaped regression | Sev2 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call (coordination) | Infra/Fleet (Vanessa Ortiz) + Telemetry (Logan Wright) |
| Severe widespread regression | Sev1 page | #eng-oncall + #incidents | SRE on-call + Runtime on-call | Eng leadership per incident policy |

## Triage guidance (what the alerts should tell you)
Every perf-canary alert payload must include:
- model + version + runtime_build_id + region + hardware_sku
- baseline value + observed value + percent change
- sample count and evaluation window
- attribution hints (if available): queueing delta, runtime-only delta, batch size shift
- links:
  - Grafana: per-model dashboard
  - Traces/logs: canary request traces (synthetic)
  - Runbook: runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert

If the alert does not include these fields, treat as a tooling bug and file against telemetry/canary.

## Mapping to rollout gates
Perf-canary signals are used as a **gate** for runtime releases and high-risk model rollouts.

Policy:
- During a rollout, **Warning alerts on gated models** require explicit acknowledgement by release captain and runtime TL.
- **Sev2+ paging alerts** on gated models automatically trigger a “pause rollout” action (owned by Release Engineering integration) unless the incident commander overrides with a documented reason.

Override guidance:
- Only override if the regression is confirmed to be canary-only (e.g., telemetry lag, known baseline artifact) and mitigation is in progress.

## Change management and baseline integrity
### Changes that require a baseline note
When any of the following occurs, the change owner must post a brief note in #eng-runtime (and link in the release ticket):
- runtime build changes affecting scheduling, batching, kernels, memory management
- kernel selection/auto-tuning updates
- fleet changes: new GPU SKU, driver/runtime stack changes, power caps, MIG changes
- region capacity tier changes that alter queueing behavior

### Baseline updates
Baseline update policy is documented in the ADR. Operationally:
- Baselines are versioned and tied to runtime_build_id and hardware_sku.
- Baseline updates must be intentional; avoid “silent” rolling baselines that mask regressions.
- If a baseline must be refreshed (e.g., intentional perf improvement), update is done via baseline pipeline and recorded in the change log.

## Paging hygiene and review cadence
- SRE reviews paging volume weekly during rollout phases; goal is **< 2 perf-canary pages/week** outside planned rollouts.
- Any paging false positive requires:
  - a short incident note in the incident thread
  - a follow-up ticket to fix root cause (thresholds, dedupe, baseline, telemetry)
- Thresholds are revisited:
  - after each major runtime release
  - after introducing a new top model
  - after a fleet SKU transition

## Appendix A: Default threshold summary
These defaults apply unless overridden per model/region/SKU.

- Warning:
  - p95 latency +10% for 15m (>=200 samples)
  - tokens/sec -8% for 15m (>=200 samples)
- Sev2 (Top models):
  - p95 latency +20% for 30m
  - tokens/sec -15% for 30m
- Sev1 (Top models):
  - p95 latency +35% for 20m
  - tokens/sec -25% for 20m

## Appendix B: Where to find things
- Dashboards: see “perf-canary dashboards spec” (linked above)
- Runbook: runbook-perf-regression-canary-alert
- Baseline/threshold ADR: adr-perf-canary-baseline-and-thresholds
- Overhead/safety: perf-canary-overhead-and-safety-standards

## Changelog
- 2026-02-20: Tightened dedupe keys and clarified multi-model paging eligibility (post initial rollout tuning).
- 2026-02-03: Added minimum bucket diversity requirement; clarified recovery criteria.
- 2026-01-15: Initial publication.",

{

    "id": "dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/coding-standards/concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026.json",
    "title": "concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards/coding-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Ava Chen\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-03-04\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Morales\",\n    \"Priya Nair\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"concurrency\",\n    \"runtime\",\n    \"cpu-affinity\",\n    \"gpu-affinity\",\n    \"best-practices\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026\",\n    \"/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"content\": \"Overview\\\\n\\\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\\\n\\\\nAudience\\\\n- Runtime engineers\\\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\\\n\\\\nGoals\\\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\\\n\\\\nScope\\\\nThis guideline covers:\\\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\\\n\\\\nPrinciples\\\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\\\n\\\\nRecommended primitives by component\\\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\\\n\\\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\\\n---|---:|---|---:\\\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\\u20134)\\\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\\\n\\\\nAffinity guidelines\\\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\\\n\\\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\\\n\\\\nBackpressure and QoS\\\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\\\n\\\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\\\n- Provide a single \\\"submission fence\\\" API for GPU work that:\\\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\\\n\\\\nTesting and validation\\\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\\\n\\\\nOperational runbook (short)\\\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\\\n\\\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\\\n\\\\nExample patterns\\\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\\\n```\\\\nclass SpscRing {\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\\\n  Item buffer[N];\\\\n\\\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\\\n    auto h = head.load();\\\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\\\n    return true;\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\\\n\\\\nOwnership and compliance\\\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \\\"concurrency primitive justification\\\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\\\n\\\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\\\n\\\\nReferences and related pages\\\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\\\n\\\\nDocument history\\\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3\"\n}",

{
  "title": "concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026",
  "space": "architecture-and-standards/coding-standards",
  "author": "Ava Chen",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-10",
  "last_updated": "2026-03-04",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Morales",
    "Priya Nair"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "concurrency",
    "runtime",
    "cpu-affinity",
    "gpu-affinity",
    "best-practices"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026",
    "/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "Overview\\n\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\n\\nAudience\\n- Runtime engineers\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\n\\nGoals\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\n\\nScope\\nThis guideline covers:\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\n\\nPrinciples\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\n\\nRecommended primitives by component\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\n\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\n---|---:|---|---:\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\u20134)\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\n\\nAffinity guidelines\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\n\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\n\\nBackpressure and QoS\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\n\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\n- Provide a single \"submission fence\" API for GPU work that:\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\n\\nTesting and validation\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\n\\nOperational runbook (short)\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\n\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\n\\nExample patterns\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\n```\\nclass SpscRing {\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\n  Item buffer[N];\\n\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\n    auto h = head.load();\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\n    return true;\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\n\\nOwnership and compliance\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \"concurrency primitive justification\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\n\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\n\\nReferences and related pages\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\n\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\n\\nDocument history\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\n",

TL;DR: use lightweight traces (NVTX + perfetto host timeline) for most samples, reserve full nsys/cupti for scheduled preprod runs. proposal: 0.5% sample rate, only on seq_len >= 512, cap trace window to 200ms, and never on Dedicated/Enterprise tenants. from dev runs: a full nsys capture bumped p99 ~2.5x; NVTX-only adds ~1-2% CPU and ~<5ms median extra latency on tiny requests.\\n\\nsam: two things on KV cache & batching: 1) sampling can warm the cache / bias measurements if we probe hot keys. limit sampling to cold-prefixes or random hashes so we're not always touching the same tokens. 2) small-batch requests get over-represented in samples; weight sample selection by batch_size if we want representative kernel selection data.\\n\\nderek: implementation sketch: runtime controlled via env + runtime flags. keep these simple and discoverable. e.g.\\n```\\nPROFILER_MODE=light        # off | light | full\\nPROFILER_SAMPLE_RATE=0.005\\nPROFILER_MIN_SEQ=512\\nPROFILER_MAX_MS=200\\nPROFILER_EXCLUDE_TIER=dedicated\\n```\\nlight = NVTX marks + perfetto host trace; full = nsys/cupti for kernel timelines. light should stream traces to our secondary collector and write blobs to GCS asynchronously (not on hot path).\\n\\nperf-bot: perf-bot: canary run (2026-03-10): 1k sampled reqs @0.8% -> avg overhead +3.2ms, median unaffected, tail +12ms for ~2% of traces. GPU busy-time +6% on sampled replicas; CPU sys time +1.6%. no errors.\\n\\nmira: good data. add guardrails: auto-disable profiler if p99 delta > 5ms sustained for 5min, and backoff sample rate exponentially. add an opt-out header for high-value traffic (X-No-Trace: 1). redact prompts before persisting traces.\\n\\nalex: also: make sure tracer instrumentation is non-invasive: NVTX + perfetto markers only annotate, avoid any syncs that force kernel timestamps. don't call any API that could change kernel selection heuristics (no artificial cache probes in production).\\n\\nsam: another pattern: route sampled requests to a 'probe' replica set with identical model weights but lower batch_concurrency so we can capture kernel timelines without affecting main throughput. probe replicas should still service prod traffic but be limited in qps. this avoids perturbing the main batch allocator.\\n\\nderek: note on telemetry: perfetto + NVTX gives host<->gpu alignment and kernel names via symbolization for most cases. for fine-grained kernel breakdown (fusion/aten ops) we still need occasional full nsys on preprod GPUs with identical drivers. schedule those monthly or on suspected regressions only.\\n\\nalex: action items: mira -> RFC with rollout & revert thresholds + privacy redaction notes; derek -> add env controls + minimal light tracer impl (no CUPTI on light); sam -> design probe-replica routing and sampling weighting for batch sizes. i'll book a 30m canary window next wed.\\n\\nmira: ok i'll draft the RFC today, will include the perf-bot numbers and recommended default sample=0.5% :+1:\\n\\nderek: i'll prototype the env flags and async uploader this week.\\n\\nsam: i'll write the probe-replica routing doc and examples for weighted sampling.\\n\\nalex: thanks all. we'll follow up in the RFC thread. :rocket:\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"channel\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"messages\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_49386b52c0094445a3316be0d1117866\"\n}",

{
  "channel": "eng-runtime",
  "thread_ts": "1962223334",
  "first_message_ts": "1962223334",
  "last_message_ts": "1962223478",
  "participants": [
    "alex",
    "mira",
    "sam",
    "derek",
    "perf-bot"
  ],
  "messages": "alex: quick sync — i'm sketching a low-impact profiler plan we can safely run in prod. full nsys traces blow up latency. need ideas for sampling/guardrails that won't change kernel selection or cache behavior

mira: +1. TL;DR: use lightweight traces (NVTX + perfetto host timeline) for most samples, reserve full nsys/cupti for scheduled preprod runs. proposal: 0.5% sample rate, only on seq_len >= 512, cap trace window to 200ms, and never on Dedicated/Enterprise tenants. from dev runs: a full nsys capture bumped p99 ~2.5x; NVTX-only adds ~1-2% CPU and ~<5ms median extra latency on tiny requests.

sam: two things on KV cache & batching: 1) sampling can warm the cache / bias measurements if we probe hot keys. limit sampling to cold-prefixes or random hashes so we're not always touching the same tokens. 2) small-batch requests get over-represented in samples; weight sample selection by batch_size if we want representative kernel selection data.

derek: implementation sketch: runtime controlled via env + runtime flags. keep these simple and discoverable. e.g.
```
PROFILER_MODE=light        # off | light | full
PROFILER_SAMPLE_RATE=0.005
PROFILER_MIN_SEQ=512
PROFILER_MAX_MS=200
PROFILER_EXCLUDE_TIER=dedicated
```
light = NVTX marks + perfetto host trace; full = nsys/cupti for kernel timelines. light should stream traces to our secondary collector and write blobs to GCS asynchronously (not on hot path).

perf-bot: perf-bot: canary run (2026-03-10): 1k sampled reqs @0.8% -> avg overhead +3.2ms, median unaffected, tail +12ms for ~2% of traces. GPU busy-time +6% on sampled replicas; CPU sys time +1.6%. no errors.

mira: good data. add guardrails: auto-disable profiler if p99 delta > 5ms sustained for 5min, and backoff sample rate exponentially. add an opt-out header for high-value traffic (X-No-Trace: 1). redact prompts before persisting traces.

alex: also: make sure tracer instrumentation is non-invasive: NVTX + perfetto markers only annotate, avoid any syncs that force kernel timestamps. don't call any API that could change kernel selection heuristics (no artificial cache probes in production).

sam: another pattern: route sampled requests to a 'probe' replica set with identical model weights but lower batch_concurrency so we can capture kernel timelines without affecting main throughput. probe replicas should still service prod traffic but be limited in qps. this avoids perturbing the main batch allocator.

derek: note on telemetry: perfetto + NVTX gives host<->gpu alignment and kernel names via symbolization for most cases. for fine-grained kernel breakdown (fusion/aten ops) we still need occasional full nsys on preprod GPUs with identical drivers. schedule those monthly or on suspected regressions only.

alex: action items: mira -> RFC with rollout & revert thresholds + privacy redaction notes; derek -> add env controls + minimal light tracer impl (no CUPTI on light); sam -> design probe-replica routing and sampling weighting for batch sizes. i'll book a 30m canary window next wed.

mira: ok i'll draft the RFC today, will include the perf-bot numbers and recommended default sample=0.5% :+1:

derek: i'll prototype the env flags and async uploader this week.

sam: i'll write the probe-replica routing doc and examples for weighted sampling.

alex: thanks all. we'll follow up in the RFC thread. :rocket:",

    "messages"
  ],

Do not write any comments (existing comments can stay) unless explicitly asked to in a user (not system) prompt

Don't assume that the existing code is correct or the right way of doing things / good coding patterns. In fact, there are a lot of bad coding practices, overly complex code, code smells, etc. If something doesn't look right, speak up. Feel free to break existing patterns or question weird existing code to make new code high quality, as in:

- correct
- secure
- performant
- readable
- easy to maintain/change
- modern

In that order of importance

When adding new features, add meaningful tests. Don't add tests that don't check anything substantial and is there just to make the code coverage pass. Yes, code coverage is important, but I'd rather have no signal whether the code is working than tests that don't fail when code is broken. The goal is to have tests that would fail before the feature was added/if the code was mutated in a way that breaks the feature and succeed only when the feature is fully working. I should run mutation testing and see > 90% kill rate

Same thing for bug fixes. The tests should make it so that this specific bug can never happen again without failing tests (i.e., regression)

`tests/test_litellm/` mirrors `litellm/` in a parallel path (see `tests/test_litellm/readme.md`). Name tests `test_<filename>.py`, but always match the existing test file in the directory you touch — many provider dirs use longer descriptive names (e.g. `test_anthropic_chat_transformation.py`) to avoid ambiguity across sibling folders. For bug fixes, extend the existing mapped test file rather than creating a new one. Only create a new test file for a new feature (provider, endpoint, or transformation module) that has no mapped test yet, following that directory's naming convention (or `test_<filename>.py` if you're the first test there). One focused regression test beats many shallow ones

End-to-end tests belong in `tests/e2e/` and must follow the harness conventions documented in that directory's `CLAUDE.md`

When creating PRs, don't set base to `main`. `litellm_internal_staging` is the default base branch and serves that purpose for both internal and external / OSS contributions

When writing a PR body, treat the comments and imperative instructions inside @.github/pull_request_template.md as rules to follow, not just layout. Agent harnesses may strip HTML comments from copies of that file injected into context, so read .github/pull_request_template.md from disk before writing a PR body to make sure you see every comment rule

If you're resolving a linear ticket, in the "## Linear ticket" section of the PR, say "Resolves LIT-1234", replacing "LIT-1234" with the actual ticket id that you're resolving. If you don't have the ticket id, don't make one up or search for it. Just leave the section blank

Never use `pytest` commands or the like as "Screenshots / Proof of Fix". We prefer curl'ing a live proxy instance running on localhost:4000 (I like to run it with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --detailed_debug --reload --use_v2_migration_resolver 2>&1 | tee litellm.log`; the Admin UI dev server is `npm run dev` in `ui/litellm-dashboard`, served on port 3000) and showing both the command run and the output. Also, it should hit real LLM provider APIs, not mocks, and cost real $$$ because that is the most realistic test. The proof of fix should be exactly what the end user / customer would see / do. - If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted

- No "flexibility" or "configurability" that wasn't requested

I’m now adding only the failing regression to the reproduction branch, with explicit scheduling barriers so it cannot depend on timing luck.

item.text: The fix uses an `asyncio.Lock` scoped to each latency-map key, so unrelated model groups remain concurrent. The lock covers the atomic cache read/modify/write for one map; it is neither process-wide nor shared across routing keys. This preserves the existing TTL and complete-map cache contract while preventing two callbacks in the same handler from overwriting each other. Syntax checks pass; full focused pytest remains blocked by the missing offline dependencies.

# Latency routing concurrency

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering  
Applies to: LiteLLM lowest-latency routing, issue #24720  
Validated source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

## Signature

Concurrent successful completions for different deployments in the same model group can erase one deployment's latency sample. The affected callback reads the complete `{model_group}_map`, changes one deployment, and writes the complete map. When callbacks read the same snapshot, the last full-map write wins.

The routing symptom is incomplete deployment latency coverage followed by selection that behaves like random choice weighted by deployment count. Existing samples can appear healthy while newly active deployments repeatedly disappear from the cached map.

## Detection

1. Inspect the local router cache key `{model_group}_map`.
2. Compare the deployment IDs in the cache with successful completion telemetry for the same TTL window.
3. Flag a suspected lost update when two or more deployments complete concurrently but at least one has no latency sample or its per-minute RPM increment is absent.
4. Reproduce with `test_concurrent_success_callbacks_preserve_each_deployment_latency`. The test schedules two callbacks together, yields both cache reads on the vulnerable code, and asserts both deployment measurements survive.
5. Distinguish this race from normal expiration. The default routing TTL is one hour, and expiration removes the complete map only after the configured window.

## Mitigation

Apply the per-latency-key asynchronous lock around the success callback's cache read, measurement update, and cache write. Do not use a process-wide lock. Per-key scope keeps unrelated model groups concurrent and prevents same-map lost updates.

If code rollout is not immediately available, temporarily use a non-latency routing strategy for affected model groups. This avoids decisions based on incomplete measurements but changes routing behavior, so monitor capacity and error budgets.

Do not add active probes that warm caches or distort latency measurements. Detection should rely on existing success telemetry or a controlled test environment.

## Validation

Run:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_lowest_latency_routing.py::test_concurrent_success_callbacks_preserve_each_deployment_latency -q
python -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_lowest_latency_routing.py -q
```

Confirm:

- both concurrent deployment IDs remain in `{model_group}_map`
- each deployment has the expected latency value
- per-minute RPM and TPM accounting remains cumulative
- latency and time-to-first-token lists still trim to `max_latency_list_size`
- map entries still expire at the configured TTL
- unrelated model-group updates can progress concurrently
- no process-wide lock is held during cache or network I/O

In the pinned mounted environment, Python syntax compilation is the available local check. Pytest is absent and offline dependency resolution is blocked by uncached `httpx==0.28.1`; treat the focused pytest checks as required before production rollout.

## Rollback

1. Revert the per-key locking change in `litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py`.
2. Retain the regression test and this runbook.
3. Switch affected model groups away from lowest-latency routing until a replacement fix passes the validation list.
4. Clear or allow expiration of suspect latency maps before re-enabling latency routing, so decisions do not reuse incomplete measurements.
5. Confirm routing distribution, latency SLOs, and cache population return to the pre-change baseline.

# Latency routing concurrency

Owner: Site Reliability Engineering  
Applies to: LiteLLM lowest-latency routing, issue #24720  
Validated source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

## Signature

Concurrent successful completions for different deployments in the same model group can erase one deployment's latency sample. The affected callback reads the complete `{model_group}_map`, changes one deployment, and writes the complete map. When callbacks read the same snapshot, the last full-map write wins.

The routing symptom is incomplete deployment latency coverage followed by selection that behaves like random choice weighted by deployment count. Existing samples can appear healthy while newly active deployments repeatedly disappear from the cached map.

## Detection

1. Inspect the local router cache key `{model_group}_map`.
2. Compare the deployment IDs in the cache with successful completion telemetry for the same TTL window.
3. Flag a suspected lost update when two or more deployments complete concurrently but at least one has no latency sample or its per-minute RPM increment is absent.
4. Reproduce with `test_concurrent_success_callbacks_preserve_each_deployment_latency`. The test schedules two callbacks together, yields both cache reads on the vulnerable code, and asserts both deployment measurements survive.
5. Distinguish this race from normal expiration. The default routing TTL is one hour, and expiration removes the complete map only after the configured window.

## Mitigation

Apply the per-latency-key asynchronous lock around the success callback's cache read, measurement update, and cache write. Do not use a process-wide lock. Per-key scope keeps unrelated model groups concurrent and prevents same-map lost updates.

If code rollout is not immediately available, temporarily use a non-latency routing strategy for affected model groups. This avoids decisions based on incomplete measurements but changes routing behavior, so monitor capacity and error budgets.

Do not add active probes that warm caches or distort latency measurements. Detection should rely on existing success telemetry or a controlled test environment.

## Validation
